Exact wording

English (as recorded here)
“It is worse to do injustice than to suffer it.”
Ancient Greek
“βούλομαι μᾶλλον ἀδικεῖσθαι ἢ ἀδικεῖν.”

“I would rather be wronged than do wrong.” The English noun-form rendering (“it is worse to do injustice than to suffer it”) converts Socrates' stated preference into a ranked claim that the interlocutor Polus immediately contests.

Attribution notes

Said by Socrates in the Gorgias, at 469b–c, and it is an argued conclusion rather than an aphorism: Polus finds it absurd and the rest of the dialogue is Socrates defending it. The line is often lifted out of that exchange and quoted as received wisdom, which loses that it was the controversial position.

How to trace any quotation to its source

Reading the cited source

The archive attributes this English wording to Plato, Gorgias 469b–c and files it under Socratic School.

What a locator tells you, and what it does not · How this archive traces a quotation

About Socrates

Socrates (c. 470/469–399 BCE) was an Athenian citizen who wrote nothing and yet redirected Greek philosophy from cosmology toward ethics and the care of the soul.

Interpretation

Socrates defends this to Callicles in the Gorgias, and it is the most counter-intuitive of his claims. His argument is that injustice damages the soul of the one who commits it, and the soul is more important than the body or property, so the doer is worse off than the victim. He also argues it is worse to escape punishment than to suffer it, on the grounds that punishment treats the damage. The position follows from taking seriously that character is what a person most fundamentally has.

Why it matters

It is testable in a specific way: consider what repeated dishonesty does to the person practising it, independent of whether they are caught.

Questions readers arrive with

What is the source of the quotation “It is worse to do injustice than to…”?

“It is worse to do injustice than to…” comes from Gorgias, 469b–c (c. 380 BCE), attributed to Socrates.

What does Socrates mean by justice?

Distributive, retributive, and restorative justice name different problems. Political philosophy asks what a just society owes its members and outsiders. This passage enters that discussion through justice, morality, courage.

Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Said by Socrates in the Gorgias, at 469b–c, and it is an argued conclusion rather than an aphorism: Polus finds it absurd and the rest of the dialogue is Socrates defending it.
